newsitem.title: FRANCE: French defence giant could upset European industry.
newsitem.headline: French defence giant could upset European industry.

text.p: French politicians seem to be dreaming aloud about a defence giant comprising almost all the country's companies in the sector but such a merger would upset the fragile balance in the European industry, defence analysts say.

Germany's Deutsche Aerospace Gmbh and Britain's British Aerospace Plc and GEC Plc are ready to deal with either Lagardere Groupe or Alcatel Alsthom winning the state's 58 percent stake in Thomson-CSF .

But a French group including Thomson-CSF, Lagardere's Matra and Alcatel with its allies Aerospatiale and Dassault Aviation -- to which Sagem and Cie des Signaux could also be added -- would be too big to handle, they say.

"There seems to be a government preference for a big "Yalta" in defence," said an industry analyst at a French brokerage. "But this seems very ambitious to me and would upset a number of alliances," he added.
The term Yalta is often used in France for stand-off agreements in industrial restructuring -- referring to the World War Two pact between Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin.
Daimler-Benz Aerospace chairman Manfred Bischoff said earlier this month that the outcome of the Thomson-CSF privatisation would be decisive for the future of the German defence industry.
In Britain, BAe and GEC might bite the bullet and merge themselves into a larger group if they have to face one large French group instead of various medium-sized companies, analysts say.

The Le Monde newspaper on Thursday cited a source at the Delegation Generale pour l'Armement (DGA) -- the top French army body -- as saying that "the next steps (in the Thomson-CSF sale) have to be acceptable for our partners."
"It would be difficult to link with the Europeans if ...British Aerospace and GEC were to merge," the paper cited its source as saying.
The source added that in Europe there was room for two missile makers and two satellite builders.

On Wednesday, the government said it wanted "the largest possible grouping of industrial capacities in order to contribute in the best possible circumstances to the restucturing of the European defence industry."

Analysts said this was one of the clearest signs yet of a wish to get the Lagardere and Alcatel camps around the table -- which could remove the need for the government to take a decision that would boost the position of one camp to the detriment of the other.

But Lagardere's Jean-Luc Lagardere and Alcatel's Serge Tchuruk, having fought each other on the issue for more than a year now, are not the closest of friends and the lumping together of the two camps would throw up lots of duplication as well as some synergies.
"It is not said that such a deal would make industrial sense," Le Monde said.
